Cross sections in {Giotto} are used to generate an in-silico cross section of a
3D dataset along an arbitrary 2D plane.

A plane may be defined in one of four ways:

`"equation"` - Provide a vector of 4 numerics to `equation`. These will be taken as the
A, B, C, D coefficients in the plane-defining function Ax + By + Cz = D

This method is shown below.

`"3 points"` - Provide 3D coordinates to `point1`, `point2`, `point3` params. For example:

```
    method = "3 points",
    point1 = c(100, 200, 300),
    point2 = c(400, 200, 300),
    point3 = c(100, 500, 700)
```

`"point and norm vector"` - Provide a 3D point anchor, then a 3D vector normal
to the plane to set the plane rotation. For example:

```
    method = "point and norm vector",
    point1 = c(100, 200, 300),
    normVector = c(0, 1, 0)  # Normal points in y direction (horizontal plane)
```

`"point and two plane vectors"` - Provide a 3D point anchor and two non-parallel
3D vectors that define the plane rotation. For example:

```
    method = "point and two plane vectors",
    point1 = c(100, 200, 300),
    planeVector1 = c(1, 0, 0),  # Vector along x-axis
    planeVector2 = c(0, 0, 1)   # Vector along z-axis
```


# Setup and load example dataset

For the example, we use a mini premade `giotto` object. This was mini dataset
is a randomly sampled subset of a STARmap mouse brain dataset.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Ensure Giotto Suite is installed
if(!"Giotto" %in% installed.packages()) {
  pak::pkg_install("drieslab/Giotto")
}

# Ensure Giotto Data is installed
if(!"GiottoData" %in% installed.packages()) {
  pak::pkg_install("drieslab/GiottoData")
}

library(Giotto)
```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# load the object
g <- GiottoData::loadGiottoMini("starmap")
```




# Create Cross Section

Next we define the cross section to create using the `"equation"` method.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
g <- createCrossSection(g,
    method = "equation",
    equation = c(0, 1, 0, 600),
    extend_ratio = 0.6,
    name = "new_cs",
    return_gobject = TRUE
)
```

# Plot cross section

This cross section can then be used in cross section-specific plotting functions.

## 2D

```{r, eval=FALSE}
crossSectionPlot(g, name = "new_cs")
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.align='center'}
knitr::include_graphics("images/cross_section/1-crossSectionPlot.png")
```

## 3D

```{r, eval=FALSE}
crossSectionPlot3D(g, 
                   name = "new_cs")
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.align='center'}
knitr::include_graphics("images/cross_section/2-crossSectionPlot3Dpng.png")
```


# Plot cross section feature plot

## 2D

```{r, eval=FALSE}
crossSectionFeatPlot(g,
                     feats = c("Mbp", "Flt1"),
                     name = "new_cs",
                     cow_n_col = 1)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.align='center'}
knitr::include_graphics("images/cross_section/3-crossSectionGenePlot.png")
```

## 3D

```{r, eval=FALSE}
crossSectionFeatPlot3D(g,
                       feats = "Mbp",
                       name = "new_cs",
                       cow_n_col = 1)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.align='center'}
knitr::include_graphics("images/cross_section/4-crossSectionGenePlot3D.png")
```
